thread_title: S. leucophylla site #2, washington Co, AL
breadcrumb: S. leucophylla site #2, washington Co, AL

posts.body_html:
Here's another site in Washington Co, AL that's similar to the previously posted site, but to the discerning eye, you can tell these plants overall look slightly different. For one, plants at site #2 look like they have little to no alata influence, and more rubra wherryi back-crossing. At the very first site, we did see one or two S. alatas and several S. rubra wherryis, whereas site #2 only contained rubra wherryis.

We didn't see any jaw-dropping red forms anywhere in Washington County, but all things considered, this red clone is still pretty nice:



Something about the shape of this trap makes it a tell-tale washington Co, AL leucophylla:



On the other hand, if I was blindfolded and then saw this plant, I had no idea it was from the same exact population. S. leucophylla var. albas were quite common at this site:



The tubular shape of this clone reminds me of S. rubra wherryi:



A regular bright white clone. Gosh, it's amazing how beautiful a plain-Jane clone can be in the wild. The most ordinary leucophylla in the wild puts most plants in our collection to shame:


The diversity here is huge:





This clone cries out rubra wherryi to me:


Overview of the field:


more photos to come!

posts.body_html:
Thanks for the ground shot Mike. Much appreciated. I found it really interesting. Appears as though the rhizome in that case is actually beneath a layer of silted material with dead plant material superimposed on that.

Tell, me: have you ever seen rhizomes from different clones growing over the top of the rhizomes of neighbouring clones in some of the dense Sarracenia populations you've visited? Or do they appear to encounter each other and then veer off in another direction? Be interested to hear from anyone who has experience of this question.

Oh, that red thing in front is the ala Mike. But, you knew that right....?
